title: BPD: The Worst Disorder or Not a Disorder at All?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore borderline personality disorder (BPD): its name and history (Adolf Stern's 1938 coinage, Otto Kernberg's later description), its classification as a cluster B personality disorder and the debate over whether it should be categorical or dimensional, the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria (five of nine), biosocial causes including childhood neglect and abuse, prevalence, splitting and black-and-white thinking, the "favorite person" dynamic, and treatment through dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) developed by Marsha Linehan, plus psychodynamic therapy. The episode closes with a listener email from Suzanne.

segments.title: Tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts promote the last three live shows of the year in Orlando, Atlanta, and Nashville, with tickets on the website.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Light opening banter about the hosts working without Jerry this week and a Bill and Ted quote.

segments.title: Introducing BPD and the mental health series
segments.summary: The hosts introduce BPD as part of their mental health series, referencing listener feedback on the emotional pain episode, and describe it as a cluster B personality disorder with a tendency toward perception-based disturbances.

segments.title: BPD versus bipolar disorder
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish BPD from bipolar disorder: bipolar has highs and lows with stable periods, while BPD involves constant emotional reactivity and is more psychological. Emotional dysregulation is named as a core hallmark.

segments.title: Self-harm and the suicide risk
segments.summary: Non-suicidal self-injury is described as a way to externalize pain. Marsha Linehan's analogy of emotional third-degree burns is cited, and the hosts note a suicide rate about fifty times the general population.

segments.title: History of the term borderline
segments.summary: Adolf Stern coined the term in 1938 to describe patients on the border between psychotic and psychoneurotic conditions. Otto Kernberg later described an unstable personality, and the diagnosis entered DSM-III about five years later.

segments.title: Stigma and the diagnostic debate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the school of thought that BPD is a cluster of symptoms rather than a personality disorder, the stigma of the diagnosis, and the DSM-5 working group's rejected proposal to make it dimensional rather than categorical.

segments.title: Marsha Linehan and radical acceptance
segments.summary: The hosts describe Marsha Linehan's late-life disclosure of her own BPD, her schizophrenia misdiagnosis and hospitalization, and her religious experience. They explain radical acceptance and how it leads to dialectical behavior therapy, the gold standard treatment that is the only proven treatment for reducing suicidal behavior.

segments.title: Biosocial causes and childhood invalidation
segments.summary: Linehan's biosocial model is explained: a biological predisposition such as executive function differences in the prefrontal cortex, combined with trigger events such as abuse, neglect, or invalidation by parents. Validating children's emotions is discussed.

segments.title: Diagnostic criteria
segments.summary: The DSM-5 nine criteria are introduced, with a diagnosis requiring five. Criteria discussed include chronic emptiness, emotional instability, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, unstable self image, impulsivity, unstable intense relationships, recurrent self-harm, paranoia or dissociation, and inappropriate anger.

segments.title: Rage as a trauma response and diagnosis challenges
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the view that BPD rage may be a response to unresolved trauma, critics who say the diagnosis pathologizes rage, and the difficulty of diagnosing BPD given overlap with anxiety, depression, PTSD, and eating disorders.

segments.title: Risk factors and family causes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss genetic links, a lousy childhood as the typical background, absent fathers and domineering mothers, parental mood disorders, and that about eighty percent of people with BPD experienced some childhood trauma.

segments.title: Chicken or egg, prevalence, and splitting
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether the disorder or parenting came first, executive function and anger, and prevalence of 0.5 to 6 percent with gender-diagnosis questions. About one in five inpatients receive a BPD diagnosis. Splitting and black-and-white thinking, including idealizing and then despising people, are described.

segments.title: Self-concept instability and identity
segments.summary: The hosts describe the instability of self-image, switching between self-confidence and self-loathing, and adopting others' interests as a way of identity-shifting, with uncertainty about where the self ends and others begin.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief mid-episode break.

segments.title: The favorite person dynamic
segments.summary: The favorite person is the one a person with BPD relies on most. The dynamic involves flattery and rage when let down, walking on eggshells, altering behavior and isolating the FP from others, and eventual burnout and abandonment.

segments.title: Splitting in favorite person relationships and regret
segments.summary: The FP may be suddenly devalued. The person with BPD often regrets the outburst and tries to win back the FP, but the cycle tends to repeat. The hosts discuss how hard it is to recognize one's own behavior as abnormal.

segments.title: Treatment outcomes and therapy approaches
segments.summary: About half of people who seek and receive treatment no longer meet criteria after five to ten years. DBT uses group skills classes with practice, distinct from movie-style group therapy, and psychodynamic therapy relating childhood experiences to present relationships.

segments.title: Therapist refusal and patient advocacy
segments.summary: Some therapists refuse BPD patients. Guidance is given that patients have a right to seek a specialist, question providers, and find a good fit.

segments.title: Finding resources and therapist shortages
segments.summary: The hosts note there are many online resources and a severe shortage of psychiatrists in the United States, with long waiting lists.

segments.title: Listener mail from Suzanne
segments.summary: Suzanne, a Dutch listener, thanks the hosts in her bachelor thesis acknowledgments for helping her stay sane, and the hosts respond warmly and invite listeners to write in.

segments.summary: Standard sign-off noting the show is a production of iHeartRadio.
